subject: pathology
title: Blood banking and transfusion medicine: core principles for exams

steps.tx: The **ABO system** is the most clinically important blood group system, because antibodies against the missing antigen are naturally present in plasma. Group O has no A or B antigen, so its plasma carries anti-A and anti-B. Group AB has both antigens and no natural antibodies, so it is the universal recipient for red cells, while group O is the universal red cell donor. The **Rh D antigen** is the next most important antigen, and anti-D is not present naturally.

steps.tx: The **Bombay phenotype** (Oh) is a rare group in which the H antigen is absent, so A and B antigens cannot be made even if the ABO genes are inherited. These people have anti-H, anti-A and anti-B in their plasma. They look like group O on routine testing, but they must receive blood from another Bombay donor. Ordinary group O blood can cause a serious haemolytic reaction in them.

steps.tx: Storage life depends on the preservative. **CPD** allows **21 days**, while **CPDA-1** extends red cell storage to **35 days** by adding adenine. **SAG-M** allows **42 days**. Packed red cells are stored at 2 to 6 degrees Celsius, and **FFP** must be kept at or below minus 25 degrees Celsius until thawed, since factors V and VIII are heat-labile. Cryoprecipitate is rich in **factor VIII**, **von Willebrand factor** and fibrinogen, making it useful for hypofibrinogenaemia.

steps.tx: **Transfusion-related acute lung injury** (TRALI) occurs within 6 hours of transfusion, usually with plasma-rich products such as FFP and platelets. It is thought to be immune mediated, often from donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies. **TACO**, by contrast, is volume overload and is not immune mediated. Irradiation prevents **transfusion-associated graft versus host disease** in at-risk patients, and leukoreduction reduces febrile reactions.
